svg.aria-label: How does a fleet turn resources into useful work under communication, coordination, and failure constraints?

a.xlink:title: The critical-path time to advance one distributed training step, including compute, exposed communication, and coordination.
Network bytes transferred per unit of local computation for a specified distributed workload.
Empirical relationships between model loss and training resources within a fitted regime.
The amount of state that can reside in a memory domain at once.
The unequal data-transfer rates within an accelerator, within a node, and between nodes.
The electrical and thermal limits on the equipment that a rack can operate concurrently.
The fixed startup component of a transfer that matters most for small messages.
The minimum aggregate link capacity across any cut that divides the cluster into two equal groups.
Queueing and contention caused when offered traffic exceeds the service capacity of shared network paths.
The staged path that reads, transforms, and delivers batches to accelerators.
Preparing future input batches while the current batch computes, subject to buffer and service-rate limits.
A completed recoverable state version persisted beyond the failure domain it is meant to survive.
An identifiable data or model version with a defined publication boundary and provenance.
A collective that reduces contributions from every participant and returns the result to every participant.
Executing eligible communication concurrently with independent compute to hide part of its elapsed cost.
Encoding gradient updates with fewer transmitted bits, with convergence and encoding costs to evaluate.
A collective that assembles the contributions of all ranks into a complete tensor at every rank.
A collective that reduces corresponding input contributions and distributes different reduced shards among ranks.
Replicating a model across workers that process distinct portions of a batch and combine their updates.
Partitioning an individual layer's tensor computation across cooperating accelerators.
Partitioning model stages across devices and scheduling microbatches through those stages.
Partitioning optimizer state, gradients, or parameters among data-parallel workers instead of keeping every state replicated.
A workload-dependent scale beyond which larger batches yield diminishing optimization progress per additional sample.
The rate at which failures interrupt a specified distributed job under stated component and correlation assumptions.
A set of saved worker states that represents one mutually compatible point in distributed execution.
Detecting and isolating failure, restoring valid state, and returning the distributed job to useful execution.
Allocating a tightly coupled job's required workers together so that partial allocation does not strand capacity.
Assigning a job's workers to physical resources according to its traffic pattern and available link hierarchy.
A selected rule for sharing feasible fleet capacity among competing users or jobs.
The fraction of fleet capacity-time that becomes useful work at the hardware ideal rate, decomposed into scheduling, runtime, and program factors.
The fraction of in-service fleet capacity-time held by complete allocations over a fixed calendar window; it does not measure work inside an allocation.
The fraction of allocated opportunity retained after execution interruptions and runtime overhead under the stated measurement contract.
The fraction of the hardware ideal rate realized by useful program operations during retained execution; distinct from progress per training example.
Progress toward a specified learning target per processed training example, distinct from useful operations per second.
The rate of completed requests that meet the stated time-to-first-token (TTFT) and time-per-output-token (TPOT) targets for a fixed request mix.
Grouping requests for shared accelerator execution to trade weight reuse against waiting time and resource demand.
Stored attention keys and values whose per-sequence growth constrains concurrent autoregressive requests.
The number of active sequences whose attention state resides in a serving replica; feasible count depends on their total cached tokens and available memory.
Combining client-trained model updates into a shared model using an explicitly defined weighting rule.
The selected set and sampling process of devices that contribute to a federated round.
A protocol that reveals an aggregate update while hiding individual contributions within its stated threat model.
The versioned definition of a deployment's task, evidence, acceptance tests, and operating limits.
Incrementally exposing live traffic to a candidate release while measuring acceptance and preserving rollback capability.
A versioned record of model artifacts, provenance, evaluations, and dependencies used for impact analysis and release control.
Adversarial manipulation of training data or updates to alter learned behavior.
A mechanism-level bound on how much a released-result distribution changes when a specified protected contribution changes.
The accumulated privacy-loss guarantee for a declared neighboring relation, sampling process, and composition rule.
A change between training or reference data and the operational data-generating distribution.
A decision rule that answers selected requests and abstains or routes the remainder under a measured risk-coverage contract.
Layered controls on source provenance, incoming data, training, and post-training behavior that reduce specified poisoning risks.
The service or human-review capacity needed to handle the rate and work of requests deferred by the primary predictor within their response deadlines.
Emissions attributed to operating energy under a stated facility boundary and grid-carbon signal.
Emissions from manufacturing and other non-operating lifecycle processes allocated to the measured system or workload.
Choosing workload time or location using a declared carbon signal while respecting deadlines, capacity, and movement costs.
The time integral of operating power across a declared set of devices and facility consumers.
A bounded deployment claim supported by evidence, controls, accountable ownership, and rules for material change.
A selected formal or normative requirement about how model outcomes or errors are distributed across affected groups.
The ability of affected people to challenge a decision and obtain investigation and an actionable remedy.
